blocks.text: Once upon a time, a king and queen had three daughters. The two older ones were pretty. But the youngest, Psyche, was so beautiful that there are no words to describe her.

People came from far and wide just to look at her. They threw flowers in her path and sang songs about her. They even said she was more beautiful than Venus, the goddess of love herself. And they stopped going to Venus's temples, because they were too busy looking at Psyche.
Venus was furious. "How dare a mortal girl steal my honors!" she said. She called her son Cupid, the winged boy whose arrows make people fall in love.
"My son," she said, "punish that girl. Make her fall in love with some horrible, ugly creature, so that she is miserable."

In Venus's garden there were two fountains, one of sweet water and one of bitter water. Cupid filled a little jar from each and flew to Psyche's room, where she lay asleep. He sprinkled a few bitter drops on her lips and touched her side with the point of his arrow.

Psyche woke up and opened her eyes. She could not see Cupid, because he was invisible. But he was so startled that he pricked himself with his own arrow! And the moment he did, he fell in love with her. Now all he wanted was to undo the harm he had done, and he poured the sweet water all over her hair.
But Venus's curse was still on Psyche. Everyone still praised her beauty, but no one asked to marry her. Her two sisters married princes, but Psyche stayed alone.

Her worried parents asked the oracle of Apollo what to do. The answer was frightening. "Your daughter will not marry a mortal man. Her husband waits for her on top of the mountain. He is a monster that neither gods nor men can resist."
Everyone wept. But Psyche was brave. "Take me to the mountain," she said. So they led her up to the mountaintop and left her there, all alone, crying with fear.

But then Zephyr, the gentle west wind, lifted her up and carried her softly down into a valley full of flowers. There she fell asleep on the grass. When she woke, she saw a grove of tall trees, and a clear fountain, and beyond it a magnificent palace with golden pillars.

She went inside. Every room was full of treasures. Then a voice spoke to her, though she could see no one. "Lady, all of this is yours. We are your servants. Rest, and bathe, and then come to supper."
The servants were invisible, but they did everything for her. A table set itself with delicious food. Invisible musicians played and sang.
Psyche's husband came to her only at night, when it was dark, and left before dawn. She never saw his face. But he was kind and gentle, and his voice was full of love, and she grew to love him.
"Please, let me see you," she begged him.
"Do not try to see me," he said. "If you saw me, you might be afraid of me, or worship me. I just want you to love me as I am."
For a while Psyche was happy. But she began to miss her family. At last her husband agreed that her sisters could come to visit. So the west wind carried them down to the valley.
When the sisters saw the golden palace and all the treasures, they were filled with jealousy. "What does your husband look like?" they asked. And at last Psyche admitted that she had never seen him.

"Don't you remember the oracle?" they said. "Your husband is a monster! The people around here say he is a huge serpent who is fattening you up so he can eat you. Take a lamp and a knife. When he is asleep, look at him, and if he is a monster, cut off his head!"

Psyche did not want to believe them. But when they had gone, she could not stop thinking about it. So that night, when her husband was asleep, she crept out of bed, picked up the lamp and lifted it high.

There, asleep, was not a monster, but the most beautiful of all the gods: Cupid himself, with golden curls and soft white wings. Psyche leaned closer to look at him. And a drop of hot oil fell from the lamp onto his shoulder.
Cupid woke up. He looked at her, and without a word, he spread his wings and flew out of the window. Psyche tried to follow him, but she fell to the ground.

Cupid stopped for a moment. "Oh, foolish Psyche," he said sadly. "Is this how you repay my love? You thought I was a monster. Go back to your sisters, since you trust them more than me. Love cannot live where there is no trust." And he flew away.
When Psyche looked around, the palace and the gardens had vanished. She was alone in an empty field.

She went to her sisters and told them everything. They pretended to be sorry, but secretly they were glad. "Maybe now he will choose one of us!" each of them thought. So the next morning, each sister climbed the mountain and called to the west wind to carry her down to Cupid's palace. But the west wind would not carry them, and they never troubled Psyche again.

Meanwhile, Psyche wandered day and night, without food or rest, searching for her husband. At last she came to a temple of Ceres, the goddess of the harvest. It was a terrible mess, with wheat and barley and tools thrown everywhere. Psyche tidied it all up, sorting everything into its proper place.
Ceres was pleased. "Poor Psyche," she said. "I cannot protect you from Venus. But here is my advice. Go to Venus yourself, and ask her to forgive you."

So Psyche went to Venus's temple. Venus was waiting for her, and she was very angry. "So you've come at last!" she said. "My son is still sick from the burn you gave him. You will have to work hard to earn my forgiveness."

She led Psyche to a storeroom, where there was a gigantic heap of grain all mixed together: wheat and barley, millet and beans and lentils. "Sort all of this into separate piles," said Venus, "before tonight." And she went off to a feast.

Psyche sat and stared at the enormous heap. It was impossible. But Cupid, who still loved her, sent help. A tiny ant came marching up, followed by a whole army of ants. Grain by grain, they sorted the heap, each kind into its own pile. Then they vanished.
When Venus came back that evening and saw the work done, she was even angrier. "You didn't do this yourself!" she said, and threw Psyche a crust of black bread for supper.
The next morning, Venus said, "Across that river there are sheep with fleece of shining gold. Bring me some of their golden wool."

Psyche went to the river. But the reeds whispered to her, "Don't cross now, Psyche. In the morning, those golden rams are fierce and dangerous. Wait until the heat of noon, when they rest in the shade. Then you'll find golden wool caught on the bushes and trees." Psyche waited, as the river god told her through the reeds, and came back with her arms full of golden wool.

But still Venus was not satisfied. "Here is a box," she said. "Take it down to the underworld, to Proserpine, the queen of the dead. Tell her that Venus would like a little of her beauty, because she has lost some of her own, looking after her sick son."

Now Psyche was sure that this would be the end of her. She climbed to the top of a high tower, in despair. But the tower itself spoke to her. "Don't give up now, Psyche, after you have come so far! I will tell you the way." And it told her how to find a cave that led down to the underworld, how to get past Cerberus, the three-headed dog, and how to get the ferryman Charon to carry her across the dark river and back.
"And one more thing," said the tower. "When Proserpine gives you the box, whatever you do, do not open it."

Psyche did everything the tower told her. She traveled safely down to the underworld, and Proserpine filled the box and gave it back to her, shut tight. Then Psyche made her way back up into the daylight.
But then she thought, "Here I am, carrying the beauty of the goddesses. Surely I could take just a tiny bit for myself, to look lovely for my husband."

So she opened the box. But there was no beauty inside. There was only a deep, magic sleep, which flew out and wrapped itself around her. Psyche fell down on the path, fast asleep, and could not wake up.

But by now Cupid's burn had healed. He missed Psyche terribly. He slipped out through a crack in his window and flew to her. He gathered up the sleep from her and shut it back inside the box, and woke her with a gentle touch of his arrow.
"Again you almost came to harm because you were too curious," he said, smiling. "Now take the box to my mother, and I will take care of everything else."
Cupid flew up to Jupiter, the king of the gods, and begged for help. And Jupiter spoke to Venus for the two of them, so kindly and so well that at last she agreed.

Then Mercury came to bring Psyche up to Mount Olympus. Jupiter handed her a cup of ambrosia, the drink of the gods. "Drink this, Psyche," he said, "and live forever. And you and Cupid will never be parted again."
So Psyche became a goddess, and she and Cupid were married at last. Later they had a daughter, and her name was Pleasure.
The name Psyche means "soul" in Greek. It also means "butterfly." That is why, in pictures, Psyche is often shown with the wings of a butterfly.
A simplified retelling of Thomas Bulfinch's “Cupid and Psyche” in The Age of Fable (1855). The original is listed under Other versions only when “Show stories with mature themes” is on in Settings.
